The hazard and the risk are easy to confuse,
because both are probabilities of an event by some time.
They answer different questions
[@hernan2020causal, Chapter 17, Section 17.2]:

> The risk and the hazard are different measures.
> The denominator of the risk—the number of individuals at baseline—is constant across times $k$
> and its numerator—all events between baseline and $k$—is cumulative.
> That is, the risk will stay flat or increase as $k$ increases.
> On the other hand, the denominator of the hazard—the number of individuals alive at $k$—varies over time $t$
> and its numerator includes only recent events—those during interval $k$.
> That is, the hazard may increase or decrease over time.

To make that comparison precise,
consider an event time $T$ that takes values in $\{1, 2, 3, \ldots\}$,
such as the follow-up interval in which an event occurs.

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-discrete-haz-risk}
#### Discrete-time hazard and risk

For $k = 1, 2, \ldots$:

- the **risk** by $k$ is
$\risk(k) \eqdef \Pr(T \le k)$,
the probability of an event in any interval up to and including $k$
among everyone at baseline;
- for each $k$ with $\Pr(T \ge k) > 0$,
so that someone is still event-free at the start of interval $k$,
the **discrete-time hazard** at $k$ is
$\haz_k \eqdef \Pr(T = k \mid T \ge k)$,
the probability of an event in interval $k$
among those still event-free at the start of interval $k$.
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-haz-vs-risk}
#### Hazard versus risk in a cohort

Suppose 1000 people are followed for four years with no censoring,
and 100, 50, 40, and 60 of them have the event in years 1 through 4.
The hazard divides each year's events by the number still event-free at the start of that year;
the risk divides the running total of events by the 1000 people at baseline:

| Year $k$ | Events | Event-free at start of $k$ | $\haz_k$ | Total events by $k$ | $\risk(k)$ |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 100 | 1000 | $100/1000 = 0.100$ | 100 | $0.10$ |
| 2 | 50 | 900 | $50/900 \approx 0.056$ | 150 | $0.15$ |
| 3 | 40 | 850 | $40/850 \approx 0.047$ | 190 | $0.19$ |
| 4 | 60 | 810 | $60/810 \approx 0.074$ | 250 | $0.25$ |

The hazard falls and then rises,
while the risk increases every year.
:::
